meta.title: Best File Sharing Apps (2026): 10 Compared, Free & Cross-Platform
meta.description: The best file sharing apps in 2026, compared on what matters: cross-platform, instant on the same Wi-Fi, a link for anyone, encrypted, free. Updated October 2026.

hero.title: The best file sharing apps in 2026
hero.body: There is no single best tool for everyone — it depends on whether you need instant transfers on the same Wi-Fi, a link anyone can open, storage that stays put, or all three. Here are the ten file sharing and file transfer apps people actually reach for, what each does well, and where each one stops.

lead: We compared the file sharing software, programs and apps people ask about most against the things that actually matter day to day: whether they cross platforms, whether the transfer is instant on the same network, whether the recipient needs to install anything, and whether your files stay private. BIShare comes out on top because it is the only one that does both jobs — fast device-to-device transfers over Wi-Fi and a browser link for anyone, anywhere — but the right pick depends on your situation, so we call out where each tool is the better choice.

table.title: At a glance

rows.r0: Works across iPhone · Android · Windows · Mac · Linux
rows.r1: Instant device-to-device on the same Wi-Fi
rows.r2: A link or code for someone on another network
rows.r4: Nothing to install on the receiving side

table.note: Checked October 2026. Quick Share: Android and Windows (Google account); recent Pixel phones can hand files to an iPhone via AirDrop; no Mac. PairDrop: browser only, pairs across networks with a code. WeTransfer free: 3 GB, 3 days. Wormhole: 10 GB, 24 hours, browser only.

0.name: BIShare
0.tag: Best overall — local speed plus a link for anyone
0.best: Best for: anyone who shares between different platforms and wants one app that works everywhere, including with people who install nothing.
0.facts: iPhone, Android, Windows, Mac, Linux, browser · free, open source (Apache 2.0) · 100 GB by link, no limit nearby · end-to-end encrypted · no account
0.body: BIShare is the only tool here that covers both cases at once. On the same Wi-Fi it sends device to device at local-network speed, end-to-end encrypted, the way AirDrop does — but between any mix of iPhone, Android, Windows, Mac and Linux. When the other person is far away, you send a link they open in any browser, no app or account on their end, up to 100 GB, encrypted before upload with the key in the link. Links expire after 6, 12 or 24 hours, whichever you pick, or after the first download if you choose. Rooms let a group drop files for each other by code, end-to-end encrypted as well. What it does not do: keep files permanently (it is a transfer tool, not a drive) or collaborate on documents.
0.cons: Not a cloud drive; a browser transfer holds the file in memory, so the very biggest files are better sent nearby.

1.name: LocalSend
1.best: Best for: privacy-minded users who only need same-network transfers and want open source.
1.facts: iPhone, Android, Windows, Mac, Linux · free, open source · same network only · encrypted device to device · no account
1.body: <goLocalsend>LocalSend</goLocalsend> is a well-loved open-source app that sends files directly between devices on the same network, encrypted, across every desktop and mobile platform. As a same-network AirDrop replacement it is excellent and fast. The trade-off is decisive for some people: there is no link route at all, so it cannot reach anyone on a different network or anyone who cannot install the app.
1.cons: Both sides need the app; no way to send to someone who is not on your Wi-Fi.

2.name: AirDrop
2.best: Best for: people who only ever share between iPhones, iPads and Macs.
2.facts: Apple devices only · built in, free · nearby only · encrypted · no account
2.body: If everyone you share with is on an iPhone, iPad or Mac, <goAirdropAlt>AirDrop</goAirdropAlt> is instant, private and already installed — hard to beat. Its one limitation is also decisive: it is Apple-only. It cannot send to an Android phone, a Windows PC or Linux, which is exactly why cross-platform tools exist.
2.cons: No Android, no Windows, no Linux, and no link for someone far away.

3.name: PairDrop (and Snapdrop)
3.best: Best for: a quick transfer with nothing installed, on a borrowed or locked-down computer.
3.facts: Any browser · free, open source · same network, or paired across networks with a 6-digit code · encrypted WebRTC · no account
3.body: PairDrop, the actively maintained successor to <goSnapdrop>Snapdrop</goSnapdrop>, runs entirely in the browser: open the same page on two devices and drag a file across. Devices on the same network see each other automatically, and unlike the original Snapdrop, PairDrop can pair two devices on different networks with a 6-digit code or a temporary public room. There are no native apps, nothing is stored, and transfers are peer to peer. On networks that isolate clients (hotels, offices) it needs the pairing route.
3.cons: No apps, no persistent link — both people have to be online at the same time.

4.name: Quick Share (Google)
4.tag: Best built-in option for Android and Windows
4.best: Best for: Android owners who also have a Windows PC and a Google account.
4.facts: Android, Windows (64-bit Windows 10+) · free · nearby only · Google account required · no Mac; iPhone only from recent Pixel phones
4.body: <goNearby>Quick Share</goNearby> is Android's built-in nearby sharing, and Google's Windows app extends it to a PC on the same network with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on. For an Android-plus-Windows household it is free and already there. It does not run on a Mac or Linux, needs a Google account signed in, and reaches an iPhone only from recent Pixel phones through AirDrop's open mode — for everything else you need a cross-platform app.
4.cons: No Mac, no Linux, account required, no link route.

5.name: Wormhole
5.tag: Best encrypted one-off link, no app
5.best: Best for: sending one file up to 10 GB privately to someone far away, from a browser.
5.facts: Any browser · free · 10 GB · end-to-end encrypted in the browser · links expire in 24 hours · no account
5.body: <goWormhole>Wormhole</goWormhole> encrypts the file in your browser before upload and puts the key in the link, so the service cannot read what you send. Files up to 5 GB are held for 24 hours; larger ones stream peer to peer, which means both browsers must stay open. It has no local route and no apps, and 10 GB is the ceiling. Within those limits it is a clean, honest tool.
5.cons: 10 GB cap, no local transfer, no apps, both sides online for big files.

6.name: WeTransfer
6.tag: The classic link service — now a tight free plan
6.best: Best for: emailing a file to a client who expects a WeTransfer link.
6.facts: Browser and apps · free plan: 3 GB per transfer, 3 days, 10 transfers a month · not end-to-end encrypted · no account to send
6.body: <goWetransfer>WeTransfer</goWetransfer> is the name people know for "upload, get a link". The free plan has shrunk: 3 GB per transfer, links that last 3 days, and a monthly cap of ten transfers or 3 GB in total. It is never instant, because everything goes through its servers, and files are not end-to-end encrypted. Fine for a document or a short video when the recipient insists on it; for anything large or private there are better free options.
6.cons: 3 GB free cap and 3-day expiry, no local route, no end-to-end encryption.

7.name: Send Anywhere
7.tag: Good cross-platform sender with a paid tier behind it
7.best: Best for: people who like the 6-digit key flow and do not mind ads.
7.facts: iPhone, Android, Windows, Mac, Linux, browser · free with ads · 10 GB by link, more by 6-digit key · not end-to-end encrypted · account for links
7.body: <goSendAnywhere>Send Anywhere</goSendAnywhere> popularised the 6-digit key: type it on the other device and the file comes across, on nearly every platform. The free tier carries ads and pushes toward a subscription, and transfers are not end-to-end encrypted. It still works well; it is simply no longer the cleanest way to do what it does.
7.cons: Ads on the free tier, no end-to-end encryption, account needed for some features.

8.name: Google Drive (and Dropbox, OneDrive)
8.tag: Best when the files should stay somewhere
8.best: Best for: teams and anyone who needs storage, versions and shared folders rather than a transfer.
8.facts: Every platform · 15 GB free (Drive), 2 GB (Dropbox), 5 GB (OneDrive) · not end-to-end encrypted · account required
8.body: A cloud drive is the right answer when the file has to live somewhere: a shared folder for a team, a document several people edit, a backup. It is the wrong answer for a one-off transfer — every byte goes up and comes back down, it uses your quota, the other person usually needs an account, and the provider can read the file. Use it for storage; use a transfer tool for transfer.
8.cons: Slow for one-offs, quota-bound, account on both sides, provider can read files.

9.name: SHAREit
9.best: Best for: almost nothing today — listed because people still search for it.
9.facts: iPhone, Android, Windows, Mac · free with ads · nearby · not end-to-end encrypted · bundled content
9.body: <goShareit>SHAREit</goShareit> pioneered cross-platform local transfer on phones, but it is now weighed down by ads, bundled content, broad permissions, and a history of security and privacy findings. It still moves files. Any of the tools above does the same job more cleanly, and most of them for free without the ads.

why.title: Why BIShare tops the list
why.body: Most tools solve half the problem. AirDrop, LocalSend and Quick Share are fast nearby but cannot reach someone on another network; WeTransfer and Wormhole reach anyone but are never instant. BIShare does both from one app — instant and end-to-end encrypted on your own network, or a 100 GB browser link for anyone — on every platform, free, open source, with no account and no ads. That combination is the whole reason it exists.

0.q: What is the best free file sharing app in 2026?
0.a: For most people, BIShare — free and open source, works across iPhone, Android, Windows, Mac and Linux, sends instantly on your local network, and gives you a 100 GB encrypted link for anyone who is not nearby. If you only need same-network transfers, LocalSend is an excellent free choice too.

1.q: What is the best file sharing app for Android?
1.a: Quick Share is built in and fine for Android-to-Android and Android-to-Windows. For an iPhone, a Mac, Linux, or anyone far away, use BIShare: it is free on Google Play, needs no account, and adds a link route. LocalSend is the open-source pick for same-network only.

2.q: What is the best file sharing app for laptops?
2.a: BIShare or LocalSend between laptops on the same Wi-Fi — both are free, cross-platform and send at local speed with nothing uploaded. PairDrop when one laptop cannot install anything. For a laptop in another place, a BIShare link up to 100 GB.

3.q: What is the best way to send files between iPhone and Android?
3.a: AirDrop cannot reach Android, so use a cross-platform app. BIShare sends directly between the two over Wi-Fi, or by link when they are apart. LocalSend also handles same-network iPhone-to-Android transfers well.

4.q: Which file sharing apps are end-to-end encrypted?
4.a: BIShare (local and link), LocalSend (device to device), AirDrop, PairDrop's browser transfers and Wormhole's links are encrypted end to end. WeTransfer, Send Anywhere, Google Drive and SHAREit are not — they use HTTPS in transit, but the service can read the file.

5.q: Do I need an account to receive a file?
5.a: With BIShare, Wormhole and PairDrop the recipient never needs an account: a link, a code or a browser page is enough. LocalSend and AirDrop need no account either, but both devices must be on the same network with the app. Quick Share needs a Google account; cloud drives usually need one on both sides.

6.q: What is the best app to transfer files from phone to PC?
6.a: On the same Wi-Fi, BIShare (any phone, any PC) or Quick Share (Android to Windows). Without Wi-Fi, turn on the phone's hotspot and use BIShare or LocalSend — the local route needs no internet. For a PC somewhere else, a BIShare link.

7.q: Which app is best for sharing large files?
7.a: Nearby, BIShare and LocalSend have no size limit — a 200 GB folder goes across at Wi-Fi speed. By link, BIShare allows 100 GB free, Wormhole 10 GB, Send Anywhere 10 GB, WeTransfer 3 GB. Cloud drives are limited by your storage quota.

8.q: What can I use instead of WeTransfer or SHAREit?
8.a: BIShare replaces both: WeTransfer-style links up to 100 GB plus instant local transfers, without ads, size caps or the privacy concerns around SHAREit. Wormhole is a good encrypted link-only alternative; LocalSend a good local-only one.

9.q: Is it safe to use free file sharing apps?
9.a: It depends on the app. Open-source tools with end-to-end encryption and no account — BIShare, LocalSend, PairDrop, Wormhole — leave nothing readable on a server. Be careful with apps that carry ads and ask for broad permissions, and with any download that promises "AirDrop for Windows" or similar: get apps from the official stores.

10.q: What is the best file sharing app for Linux, including Ubuntu?
10.a: BIShare and LocalSend both run on Linux and send to phones, Windows PCs and Macs on the same network. BIShare offers a .deb for Ubuntu and Debian, an AppImage and a tar.gz on its GitHub releases page; LocalSend is on Flathub. Linux Mint ships Warpinator for transfers between Linux machines. Of these, only BIShare also makes a link for someone on another network.

11.q: What is the difference between a file sharing app and a file transfer app?
11.a: The two names overlap. A file transfer app moves a copy from one device to another and is finished: BIShare, LocalSend, AirDrop, Quick Share and Send Anywhere work this way. File sharing also covers storage that stays put for several people to open, such as Google Drive, Dropbox and OneDrive. This guide ranks both kinds and says which is which.

12.q: Which file sharing app is the fastest?
12.a: On the same network, any app that sends device to device: BIShare, LocalSend, AirDrop or Quick Share reach 40 to 110 MB/s over Wi-Fi 5 and Wi-Fi 6 in our measurements. Anything that uploads first, including every link service and cloud drive, is limited by your upload speed.

13.q: What is the best P2P file sharing app?
13.a: For devices on one network, BIShare or LocalSend, which run on every platform and send directly with nothing uploaded. Across the internet, PairDrop or BIShare's browser tool pair two devices with a code and connect them directly, using a relay only when the direct path is blocked.

14.q: What is the best file sharing software for a team?
14.a: For documents a team edits together, a cloud drive: Google Drive (15 GB free), Dropbox (2 GB) or OneDrive (5 GB), each with shared folders and about 30 days of version history on the free plan. A transfer app such as BIShare is for sending a copy, not for keeping one.

speed.title: Which file sharing app is the fastest?
speed.body: Speed depends far more on the route than on the brand. An app that sends device to device on your own network is limited by Wi-Fi; one that uploads to a server is limited by your internet line.

0.h: Fastest: device to device on the same network
0.b: BIShare, LocalSend, AirDrop and Quick Share all send straight from one device to the other. On current hardware we measure 40–50 MB/s over Wi-Fi 5 and 70–110 MB/s over Wi-Fi 6, so a 10 GB folder takes two to four minutes. The radio sets the pace, which is why these four land in the same range.

1.b: A link from BIShare, Wormhole or WeTransfer, and a folder in Google Drive, Dropbox or OneDrive, has to climb your upload line before anyone can download it. At a 40 Mbps upload that is about 5 MB/s, so the same 10 GB needs over half an hour, however fast the service is.

2.h: What decides it for a team
2.b: Collaboration suites feel fast because files sync in the background while you keep working. For the first upload of a large video they are bound by the same upload speed as any link.

p2p.title: P2P file sharing apps: which of these are peer to peer
p2p.body: Peer to peer means the file travels from one device to the other without being stored on a company's server. It has nothing to do with torrent networks; here it describes a private transfer between two devices you choose.

0.h: Peer to peer on one network
0.b: BIShare, LocalSend, AirDrop and Quick Share send directly between devices that are close together. Nothing is uploaded, and the transfer works with the internet switched off.

1.h: Peer to peer across the internet
1.b: PairDrop connects two browsers directly with WebRTC and falls back to a relay when a network blocks the direct path. BIShare's browser tool pairs two devices on different networks with a six-character code in the same way. Wormhole switches to a peer-to-peer transfer for files over 5 GB, and Send Anywhere's six-digit key sends directly while both sides stay online.

2.b: WeTransfer, Wormhole links under 5 GB, BIShare links, Send Anywhere links and every cloud drive store the file on a server until it is downloaded or expires. That is what lets the recipient collect it later, and it is why encryption matters more on this route.

3.b: For two devices in the same room, any of the first group; BIShare and LocalSend are the two that cover every platform. For someone far away who is online right now, a paired browser transfer. For someone who will download tomorrow, a link.

teams.title: File sharing software for teams: when the files have to stay put
teams.body: Transfer tools move a copy and forget it. A team that edits the same documents all week needs the opposite: storage, a history of changes and control over who can open what. BIShare does none of that, and the three services below do.

0.b: 15 GB free, shared with Gmail and Google Photos. Each person is a Viewer, a Commenter or an Editor, and a file can be limited to named people or opened to anyone with the link. For uploaded files such as PDFs, Google may delete an old version after 30 days or once 100 newer versions exist, unless you mark it to be kept.

1.b: 2 GB free. Its strength is the synced folder that looks the same on every computer. Dropbox keeps previous versions for 30 days on the Basic, Plus and Family plans and for 180 days on Professional, Essentials, Business and Standard.

2.b: 5 GB free, and built into Windows and Microsoft 365. Microsoft retains a file's version history for 30 days, for every file type, though an administrator can turn versioning off on a work or school account.

3.h: Where a transfer app still fits
3.b: Even inside a team, a 40 GB video export or a folder for a client who has no account is a transfer, not a collaboration. Send it with a transfer app and keep the working documents in the drive.

safety.title: Sharing sensitive files: what to check first
safety.body: Every service on this list says it is secure. Four questions separate the ones that are from the ones that only use HTTPS.

0.h: Can the service read the file?
0.b: With end-to-end encryption it cannot. BIShare, LocalSend, AirDrop, PairDrop and Wormhole encrypt so that only the two ends hold the key. WeTransfer, Send Anywhere, Google Drive and SHAREit protect the connection with HTTPS, and the provider can still open what it stores.

1.h: How long does the file exist?
1.b: A BIShare link expires after 6, 12 or 24 hours, as the sender chooses, or after the first download. Wormhole links last 24 hours, Send Anywhere links 48 hours and WeTransfer's free links three days. A file in a cloud drive stays until someone deletes it.

2.b: With BIShare and Wormhole the key is part of the link itself, so the link is the secret: send it through a channel you trust. WeTransfer lets you add a password to a transfer on every plan, the free one included. In Google Drive you can restrict a file to named accounts, which is the stronger control when every recipient has one.

3.h: What else does the app take?
3.b: Open-source apps can be inspected, and BIShare, LocalSend and PairDrop are open source. Ad-supported apps earn from attention and data: when we checked in October 2026, SHAREit's own data safety section on Google Play said its data is not encrypted. Read that section before installing any sharing app.
